question: What is the primary function of a spinal reflex?

options.A: To store long-term memory in the spinal cord
options.B: To provide quick protection against bodily harm
options.C: To regulate conscious thought processes in the brain
options.D: To coordinate voluntary movements of the limbs

explanation: Spinal reflexes act fast to protect the body from sudden injury before the brain even processes the pain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h1)

question: Why do spinal reflexes occur faster than voluntary movements?

options.A: They bypass processing in the brain for immediate action
options.B: They rely on hormonal transport through the bloodstream
options.C: They use larger nerve fibers exclusively found in legs
options.D: They depend on conscious decisions made by the spinal cord

explanation: Integrating the response entirely within the spinal cord saves precious milliseconds by avoiding transmission to the brain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h1)

question: Which nerve fiber carries sensory signals into the spinal cord?
explanation: Afferent sensory neurons bring electrical impulses from peripheral receptors into the dorsal region of the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h2)

question: A patient steps on a nail and immediately jerks their foot away. What structure acts as the effector in this reflex?

options.A: The flexor muscles of the leg
options.B: The sensory nerve endings in the foot
options.C: The integration center in the brain
options.D: The pain receptors in the skin

explanation: Muscles serve as effectors because they contract to pull the limb away from the painful stimulus. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h2)

question: What is the specific sensory receptor involved in the stretch reflex?
explanation: Muscle spindles are embedded within skeletal muscle fibers to detect stretching and changes in muscle length. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h3)

question: What happens to the antagonist muscle during a normal stretch reflex?
explanation: Reciprocal inhibition ensures that the antagonist muscle relaxes so the stretched muscle can contract effectively without resistance. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h3)

question: What is the main physiological role of the Golgi tendon reflex?

options.A: To detect changes in environmental temperature on the skin
options.B: To prevent muscle and tendon injury from excessive tension
options.C: To maintain normal resting muscle tone during sleep
options.D: To accelerate the speed of voluntary limb movements

explanation: Golgi tendon organs monitor tension and trigger relaxation to protect musculoskeletal tissues from tearing under heavy loads. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h4)

question: How does the Golgi tendon reflex differ functionally from the stretch reflex?

options.A: It promotes muscle relaxation during high tension rather than contraction
options.B: It responds exclusively to cold temperatures instead of physical force
options.C: It operates entirely within the brain rather than the spinal cord
options.D: It involves only a single synapse instead of multiple interneurons

explanation: High tension activates the Golgi tendon organ to inhibit the motor neuron, causing relaxation, whereas the stretch reflex causes contraction. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h4)

question: What is the purpose of the crossed extensor reflex?

options.A: To increase blood flow to the site of an injury
options.B: To transmit pain signals directly to the cerebral cortex
options.C: To maintain balance by extending the opposite limb
options.D: To pull the injured limb away from a sharp object

explanation: The crossed extensor reflex supports body weight on the uninjured side when the other limb withdraws from danger. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h5)

question: Which characteristic is typical of a flexor withdrawal reflex?

options.A: It involves multiple synapses and interneurons
options.B: It uses a single monosynaptic connection
options.C: It occurs entirely without sensory input
options.D: It affects only muscles on the same side of injury

explanation: Withdrawal reflexes are polysynaptic, requiring interneurons to coordinate complex muscle groups for effective limb retraction. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h5)

question: What does absent or severely diminished reflex testing usually indicate?
explanation: Hyporeflexia or areflexia suggests a disruption along the lower motor pathway, such as peripheral nerve damage. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h6)

question: A patient exhibits brisk, exaggerated knee-jerk reflexes with involuntary muscle beating. What term describes this finding?
explanation: Exaggerated reflexes point to hyperreflexia, which commonly results from upper motor neuron damage releasing inhibitory control. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T27#GNS211_U3_T27_h6)
